Nayib Bukele: President of El Salvador since 2019. Nayib Armando Bukele Ortez (born 24 July 1981) is a Salvadoran politician and businessman who has served as the 43rd president of El Salvador since 2019.
Formed from the union of Deira and Bernicia, this early medieval English kingdom once stretched from the Humber all the way to the Firth of Forth — which kingdom?
Northumbria: Medieval English kingdom. Northumbria was an early medieval English kingdom, existing between 654 and 1066 AD, spanning modern-day Northern England and Southern Scotland.
This Austrian-born SS commando led the Gran Sasso raid that freed Mussolini from captivity and later advised Egypt's Gamal Abdel Nasser after fleeing to Franco's Spain — who was he?
This British explorer and his eldest son vanished in 1925 hunting an ancient lost city he was convinced lay hidden in the Amazon rainforest — who was he?
Percy Fawcett: British explorer and military officer.
Auguste Comte pioneered this 19th-century philosophy holding that all genuine knowledge comes from logic and sensory experience, dismissing intuition and faith — what is it?
An Indian politician born in 1970, this member of the Indian National Congress serves as the 12th leader of the Opposition in Lok Sabha and represents Rae Bareli. Who is he?
Rahul Gandhi: 12th Leader of the Opposition in Lok Sabha since 2024.
He made his film debut as the boozy title character in a 1987 comedy, then decades later earned an Oscar nomination for playing Jack Hock in Can You Ever Forgive Me? — who is he?
Born in Newcastle upon Tyne to Russian émigré parents, this KGB spy ring leader in New York was arrested by the FBI on espionage charges in 1957 — who was he?
Prince Gustaf Adolf, Duke of Västerbotten
In October 2025, she became the first woman ever to serve as Prime Minister of Japan — who is she?
Sanae Takaichi: Prime Minister of Japan since 2025. Takaichi's administration has consistently polled high in approval ratings.
A close friend of Stalin who rose to lead the Communist Party in Leningrad, his 1934 assassination at the Smolny Institute became Stalin's pretext for the Great Purge — who was he?
Sergei Kirov: Soviet politician and revolutionary (1886–1934)
During the War of the Spanish Succession in 1706, Prince Eugene of Savoy's relief of this besieged Savoyard capital — and the death of hero Pietro Micca — became legend; what's this military event?
Siege of Turin: 1706 battle of the War of the Spanish Succession. The Siege of Turin, June to September 1706, took place during the War of the Spanish Succession.
A former U.S.-based banker who once backed a rival political party, this businessman scored a surprise win in Syriza's 2023 leadership election before founding his own party — who is he?
Born in Doha in 1980, this man only became heir after an older brother renounced the throne — and he's reigned over his Gulf nation since 2013. Who is he?
Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani: Emir of Qatar since 2013.
At just 33, this Marxist revolutionary became president after a coup staged on his behalf, then launched sweeping reforms he called the people's democratic revolution — who is he?
Thomas Sankara: President of Burkina Faso from 1983 to 1987.
The first Asian to lead the United Nations, this Burmese diplomat served a record ten years and one month as Secretary-General starting in 1961 — who was he?
U Thant: UN Secretary-General from 1961 to 1971.
Posthumously awarded India's highest military honor, the Param Vir Chakra, this army captain died fighting Pakistani troops at Point 4875 during the Kargil War in 1999 — who is he?
Vikram Batra: Indian Army officer, recipient of Param Vir Chakra (1974–1999)
Launched by the United States after the September 11 attacks, this global campaign targeted al-Qaeda, the Taliban, and later Iraq's Ba'athist regime — what was it called?
War on terror: Military campaign following the September 11 attacks.

Deported to Siberia by the NKVD as a young man, this Polish general later imposed martial law as military dictator in 1981 and went on to serve as his country's last communist-era leader and briefly its president — who is he?
Wojciech Jaruzelski: Leader of Poland from 1981 to 1989.
This Japanese samurai, who lived from 1574 to 1607, served as daimyō of the Fukui Domain in Echizen during the transition into the Edo period — who is he?
Yūki Hideyasu: Japanese samurai. Yūki Hideyasu (結城 秀康; 1 March 1574 – 2 June 1607) was a Japanese samurai who lived during the Azuchi–Momoyama and early Edo periods.
Which one below was born first?
Joseph Schumpeter (born 1883) is the earliest of the four. Joseph Alois Schumpeter (German: [ˈʃʊmpeːtɐ]; February 8, 1883 – January 8, 1950) was an Austrian political economist.
Which of these people was born first?
Omar Khayyam (born 1048) is the earliest of the four.
Which one below was established earliest?
COBOL (founded 1959) is the earliest of the four.
MATLAB (founded 1984) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these is an astronomer?
Nancy Roman is an astronomer. Nancy Grace Roman (May 16, 1925 – December 25, 2018) was an American astronomer who made important contributions to stellar classification and stellar motions.
Which one below is best known as a mathematician?
Omar Khayyam is a mathematician. Omar Khayyam (1048–1131) was a Persian poet and polymath, known for his contributions to mathematics, astronomy, philosophy, and Persian literature.
What is the atomic number of Iodine?
Iodine is a chemical element; it has symbol I and atomic number 53.
What is the atomic number of Cobalt?
Cobalt is a chemical element; it has symbol Co and atomic number 27.
In what year was Ken Jennings born?
Ken Jennings: Kenneth Wayne Jennings III (born May 23, 1974) is an American game show host and author who has hosted the syndicated quiz show Jeopardy! since 2021.
In what year was Valentina Tereshkova born?
Valentina Tereshkova: Valentina Vladimirovna Tereshkova (born 6 March 1937) is a Russian engineer, politician, and former Soviet cosmonaut.
In what year was Katalin Karikó born?
Katalin Karikó: Karikó laid the scientific groundwork for mRNA vaccines, overcoming major obstacles and skepticism in the scientific community.
In what year did Harold Shipman die?
Harold Shipman: Harold Frederick Shipman (14 January 1946 – 13 January 2004) was an English doctor in general practice and serial killer.
In what year did Aristotle die?
Aristotle (Ancient Greek: Ἀριστοτέλης, romanized: Aristotélēs; 384–322 BC) was an ancient Greek philosopher and polymath.
In what year was Angelman syndrome discovered?
Angelman syndrome (AS) is a rare genetic disorder that affects approximately 1 in 15,000 individuals.

Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-19: Russian Aircraft Corporation MiG. The Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-19 (Russian: Микоян и Гуревич МиГ-19; NATO reporting name: Farmer) is a Soviet second generation, single-seat, twinjet fighter aircraft.
Yakovlev MC-21: United Aircraft Corporation. The aircraft made its maiden flight on 28 May 2017 from Irkutsk.
Which country is McDonnell Douglas F-15E Strike Eagle from?

McDonnell Douglas F-15E Strike Eagle: United States. The McDonnell Douglas (now Boeing) F-15E Strike Eagle is an American all-weather multirole strike fighter derived from the McDonnell Douglas F-15 Eagle.
Who is credited with discovering Nihonium?
Nihonium: Joint Institute for Nuclear Research. Nihonium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Nh and atomic number 113.
Who is credited with discovering Mass–energy equivalence?
Mass–energy equivalence: Albert Einstein. In physics, mass–energy equivalence is the relationship between mass and energy in a system's rest frame.
Who is credited with discovering Plesiosaurus?
Plesiosaurus: Mary Anning. It is known by nearly complete skeletons from the Lias of England.
Which European four-engine turboprop military transport plane, sized between the Lockheed C-130 and Boeing C-17, can land on rough airstrips and double as an aerial refueling tanker?
Airbus A400M Atlas is a European four-engine turboprop military transport aircraft. It can carry heavier loads than the C-130 and can use rough landing strips.
From a Greek word meaning 'dissection,' which old branch of natural science is paired with physiology to study living things' structure and function?
Anatomy (from Ancient Greek (anatom) 'dissection') is the branch of morphology concerned with the study of the internal and external structure of organisms and their parts.
Considered a visual art even though it leans on civil engineering, this discipline gives us cultural symbols that often outlast the civilizations that built them. What is it?
Architecture is the study and practice of designing structures, especially habitable ones.
This Ukrainian poet and artist's collection Kobzar is considered the foundation of modern Ukrainian literature, and to some degree the modern Ukrainian language itself. Who is he?
Barracuda is a large, predatory, ray-finned, saltwater fish of the genus Sphyraena, the only genus in the family Sphyraenidae, which was named by Constantine Samuel Rafinesque in 1815.
So dense that not even light can escape its gravity, this astronomical object's boundary of no return is called the event horizon — name it?
Black hole is an astronomical body so compact that its gravity prevents anything, including light, from escaping.
Splitting from the windpipe at the carina into a right and left branch, this airway keeps forking into ever-smaller tubes until it's too narrow for cartilage support — what is it?
Bronchus (pl.: bronchi) is a passage or airway in the lower respiratory tract that conducts air into the lungs.
Also called meridian fennel, this biennial plant in the carrot family is native to western Asia, Europe, and North Africa — name it?
Caraway (Carum carvi), also known as meridian fennel, is a biennial plant in the family Apiaceae, native to western Asia, Europe, and North Africa.
Her famous experiment proved that parity is not conserved — yet the 1957 Nobel went to two male colleagues while she earned the first-ever Wolf Prize in Physics. Which Manhattan Project physicist?

Chien-Shiung Wu (pinyin: W Jinxing; May 31, 1912 - February 16, 1997) was a Chinese-American particle and experimental physicist who made significant contributions in the fields of nuclear and particle physics.

Native to tropical Africa and Asia, this genus of flowering shrubs and small trees in the Rubiaceae family produces caffeine-rich seeds that are roasted and ground into a beloved beverage worldwide — which genus?
Coffea is a genus of flowering plants in the family Rubiaceae. The seeds of some species, called coffee beans, are roasted and ground to brew into various coffee beverages.
Affecting roughly 1 in 22,000 births and more common in girls, which genetic condition caused by a chromosome 5 deletion takes its French name from a feline-sounding cry?
Cri du chat syndrome is a rare genetic disorder due to a partial chromosome deletion on chromosome 5.
With interlocking neck vertebrae that prevent almost any head movement, which genus of prehensile-tailed marsupials is commonly called the large American opossums?
Didelphis is a genus of New World marsupials.
Born in North Carolina in 1983, this former NSA contractor leaked classified files exposing global surveillance programs after working for the CIA, Dell, and a defense contractor — name him?

Edward Snowden (born June 21, 1983) is a former United States National Security Agency (NSA) intelligence contractor who leaked classified documents revealing the existence of global surveillance programs.
Co-founder of MIT's J-PAL poverty lab, she shared a 2019 Nobel with her husband and Michael Kremer for using randomized trials against global poverty — who is it?

Esther Duflo (born 25 October 1972) is a French-American economist currently serving as the Abdul Latif Jameel Professor of Poverty Alleviation and Development Economics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT).

In English its plural is the same word for many individuals but changes form when you mean many species — a quirk of this gill-bearing, cold-blooded vertebrate that lacks limbs with digits. What is it?
Fish is an aquatic, anamniotic, gill-bearing vertebrate animal with a tough cranium to protect the brain, but lacking limbs with digits.
Caused by certain strains of HPV, this sexually transmitted skin growth can appear flat or raised, sometimes clustering into a cauliflower-like shape — what condition is it?
Genital wart are a sexually transmitted infection caused by certain types of human papillomavirus (HPV).
Flown by both the U.S. Navy and Britain's Royal Navy under the name Martlet, this 1940 carrier fighter went toe-to-toe with the Mitsubishi Zero over the Pacific — which aircraft?
Grumman F4F Wildcat is an American carrier-based fighter aircraft that entered service in 1940 with the United States Navy and the British Royal Navy.

Named from the Greek for 'different wings' because most species have forewings that are part membrane, part hardened shell, this group of 40,000 insect species is the one most consistently called 'true bugs' — name this insect group?
Heteroptera are a group of about 40,000 species of insects in the order Hemiptera.
This birth defect, found in roughly one in every 250 newborn boys, involves an opening that fails to form in its typical location — what condition is this?

Hypospadias is a common malformation in fetal development, most commonly noticed in penises, in which the urethra does not open from its usual location on the head of the penis, or the middle of the vulva.
This Mexican neurophysiologist studied shamanism, meditation, and telepathy through the scientific method, writing more than 50 books before vanishing in December 1994 — who is he?
Jacobo Grinberg (born Mexico City in 1946) was a Mexican neurophysiologist and psychologist.

This 20th-century Peruvian writer of mestizo descent composed novels, poems, and stories in both Spanish and Quechua, and even coined a new literary idiom to render Indigenous perspective more authentically — who is he?
José María Arguedas (Spanish) was a Peruvian novelist, poet, and anthropologist.
This broadly distributed genus of spiders is informally grouped under a nickname referencing marital loss, encompassing both black and brown members — what is its scientific name?
Latrodectus is a broadly distributed genus of spiders informally called the widow spiders, with several species that are commonly known as the true widows.
Known mainly from fossils in Peru's Pisco Formation, this Miocene-era macroraptorial sperm whale takes its name from a biblical sea monster — what is it called?
Livyatan is an extinct genus of highly predatory macroraptorial sperm whale, containing one known species: L. melvillei.
Its Spanish name translates to 'little apple of death' — this tropical tree's apple-like fruit and toxic milky sap make it one of the most poisonous trees on Earth — which tree?
Manchineel (Hippomane mancinella), also known as the tree of death, is a species of flowering plant in the spurge family (Euphorbiaceae).
Its three main jobs are converting food into usable energy, building macromolecules like proteins and lipids, and excreting waste — the chemistry that keeps every living thing alive. What is it?
Metabolism (from) refers to the set of life-sustaining chemical reactions that occur within living organisms.
This fast-growing, drought-resistant tree native to northern India earns nicknames like 'drumstick tree' and 'horseradish tree,' and its leaves and seed pods are eaten as vegetables. What is it?
Moringa oleifera is a short-lived, fast-growing, drought-resistant tree of the family Moringaceae, native to northern India and used extensively in South and Southeast Asia.

Encompassing three distinct genetic conditions marked by nervous-system tumors, one type brings café au lait skin spots and scoliosis while another causes early-onset hearing loss and cataracts — which condition?
Neurofibromatosis (NF) refers to a group of three distinct genetic conditions in which tumors grow in the nervous system.
Beginning in the embryo and maturing a primary oocyte into a fertilization-ready egg cell, what is this reproductive process called?
Oogenesis is the differentiation of the ovum (egg cell) into a cell competent to further develop when fertilized.
Named for the extra copy of chromosome 13 found in affected cells, this condition — related to Down and Edwards syndromes — disrupts normal organ development — which syndrome?
Patau syndrome is a syndrome caused by a chromosomal abnormality, in which some or all of the cells of the body contain extra genetic material from chromosome 13.
Its name comes from the Greek for 'love of wisdom,' and physics and psychology were once branches of it — what is this rational inquiry into existence and knowledge?

Philosophy (from Ancient Greek philosophia, lit. 'love of wisdom') is a systematic study of general and fundamental questions concerning topics like existence, knowledge, mind, reason, language, and value.

This category of polymers, most commonly known in the form of PET, is prized for clothing but — unlike some of its naturally occurring plant and insect cousins — rarely biodegrades — what material is it?
Polyester is a category of polymers that contain one or two ester linkages in every repeat unit of their main chain.
Its biological practitioners link it to neuroscience while its social scientists study groups, all in service of studying the mind and behavior — what is this academic discipline?
Psychology is the scientific study of the mind and behavior. Psychology is an academic discipline of broad scope, crossing the boundaries between the natural and social sciences.
One of the three ancient arts of discourse alongside grammar and logic, this discipline studies the techniques speakers and writers use to inform, persuade, and motivate an audience — what is it?
Rhetoric is the art of persuasion.
Which plant genus in the mint family, comprising nearly 1,000 species of shrubs and perennials, includes both a common cooking herb and — surprisingly — rosemary as one of its species?
Salvia is the largest genus of plants in the sage family Lamiaceae, with just under 1,000 species of shrubs, herbaceous perennials, and annuals.
Until 2010, this pungent little cultivar of the onion was classified as its own species before being folded back into the common onion — name this allium?
Shallot is a cultivar group of the onion. Until 2010, the (French red) shallot was classified as a separate species, Allium ascalonicum.
This circular muscle normally maintains constriction of a natural body passage, relaxing only as physiological function requires — what is it called?
Sphincter is a circular muscle that normally maintains constriction of a natural body passage or orifice and relaxes as required by normal physiological functioning.
Encompassing domestic pigs and their ancestor the Eurasian wild boar, this genus within the even-toed ungulate family Suidae is native across Eurasia and Africa — which genus?

Sus (genus) is the genus of domestic and wild pigs, within the even-toed ungulate family Suidae. Sus includes domestic pigs (Sus domesticus) and their ancestor, the common Eurasian wild boar (Sus scrofa), along with various other species.

Governed by four fundamental laws relating heat, work and temperature to energy and entropy, this branch of physics underpins chemical, mechanical and biochemical engineering alike — which field of physics?
Thermodynamics is a branch of physics that deals with heat, work, and temperature, and their relation to energy, entropy, and the physical properties of matter and radiation.
One of the earliest arthropod groups ever to appear in the fossil record, this extinct marine creature persisted in the oceans for nearly 270 million years across over 22,000 species — what is it?
Trilobite (meaning "three-lobed entities") are extinct marine arthropods that form the class Trilobita.
Its wild form is dioecious while domesticated versions bear hermaphrodite flowers — this Mediterranean-native plant is the ancestor of nearly all wine and table varieties — what species?

Vitis vinifera is a species of flowering plant, native to the Mediterranean region, Central Europe, and southwestern Asia, from Morocco and Portugal north to southern Germany and east to northern Iran.
Almost always found combined with lanthanide minerals and never on its own in nature, this element with symbol Y is a key ingredient in the phosphors used inside LEDs — which element?
Yttrium is a chemical element; it has symbol Y and atomic number 39.

The only legitimate child of the poet Lord Byron, this English mathematician saw that Charles Babbage's analytical engine could do far more than crunch numbers — earning her a reputation as the first computer programmer. Who was she?
Shining as the brightest star in Taurus some 67 light-years from Earth, this red giant has swollen to roughly 45 times the Sun's size despite a cooler surface — which star?
Aldebaran: Taurus Brightest Star. Aldebaran (Arabic: الدَّبَرَان, lit. 'The Follower') is a star in the zodiac constellation of Taurus.
Used to treat dangerous heart rhythms like ventricular fibrillation, which drug can take weeks to work when swallowed but carries risks of lung, liver, thyroid, and eye toxicity?
Awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2008 for his AIDS-relief work on PEPFAR, this immunologist directed the U.S. allergy and infectious-disease institute from 1984 to 2022. Who is he?
A notoriously toxic metalloid and pnictogen with atomic number 33, it's used in lead alloys for car batteries and ammunition and as a semiconductor dopant — which element is it?
Arsenic: Chemical element with atomic number 33 (As). It is a metalloid and one of the pnictogens, and therefore shares many properties with its group 15 neighbors phosphorus and antimony.
This slender projection of a nerve cell typically carries electrical impulses away from the cell body toward other neurons, muscles, or glands — what is it called?
Axon: Long projection on a neuron that conducts signals to other neurons.
A colorless, sweet-smelling liquid hiding in petroleum, this ring-shaped hydrocarbon helps give gasoline its distinctive aroma — what is it?
Despite being just 12 to 20 cm long, this small marine creature's vivid markings flash brighter when it feels threatened, and its bite delivers a neurotoxin called tetrodotoxin — what is it?
Blue-ringed octopus: Four species of mollusk.

This tropical tree's moderately ripe flesh, once cooked, is said to taste like a fresh-baked loaf with a potato-like flavor, and 18th-century navigators carried it in seedless form to the Caribbean — what is it?
Breadfruit: Edible fruit-bearing tree in family. Moraceae.
This intensely sour citrus hybrid — a cross between a kumquat and likely a mandarin orange — is a staple of Philippine cooking and also popular in Malaysian and Indonesian cuisine — which fruit?
Calamansi: Hybrid species of citrus. Calamansi (Citrus × microcarpa), also known as calamondin, Philippine lime, or Philippine lemon, is a citrus hybrid cultivated predominantly in the Philippines.
Extracted from the cochineal insect, this bright-red pigment is also known by the food-additive code E120 — what is it called?
Carmine: Pigment, aluminium salt of carminic acid.
The biochemist hailed as the "father" of industrial fermentation, instrumental in the 1917 Balfour Declaration, became the first president of Israel — who was he?
Chaim Weizmann: Israeli statesman and British chemist (1874–1952)
Native to the Andean forests of South America, this genus of trees is nicknamed the 'fever tree' because its bark yields quinine, the only effective malaria treatment for centuries — what is it?
Cinchona: Genus of plants, source of quinine.
Used to treat gout, familial Mediterranean fever, and pericarditis, this medication has such a narrow therapeutic index that its injectable form was pulled from the US market in 2008. What is it?
Colchicine: Medication mainly used to treat gout. The American College of Rheumatology recommends colchicine, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) or steroids in the treatment of gout.

Describing how closely two variables move together, this statistical measure is famously not proof of causation, and two variables can even be linked this way without truly depending on each other — what is it called?
Correlation: Statistical relationship. In statistics, correlation is a type of statistical relationship between two random variables or bivariate data.
Making up about 80 percent water and mostly colorless, this catch-all term covers everything inside a cell's outer membrane except its nucleus — what is it?
Cytoplasm: All of the contents of a cell including organelles but excluding the nucleus.

Marked by deep gasping breaths and breath that smells oddly fruity or like acetone, this life-threatening condition arises when a shortage of insulin forces the body to burn fat into acidic ketones — what is it?
Diabetic ketoacidosis: Medical condition. Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is a potentially life-threatening acute complication of diabetes mellitus.
The tallest of the three camel species, standing up to 2.4 meters at the shoulder, which animal carries a single hump of fat on its back?
Native to southern India, this ginger-family plant produces the aromatic seeds used in both sweet and savory cooking — what is it, botanically?
Elettaria cardamomum: Species of flowering plant.
This fibromuscular tube carries food from throat to stomach using peristaltic contractions, and its name traces to Ancient Greek roots meaning roughly 'I carry what I ate.' What is it?
Esophagus: Vertebrate organ through which food passes to the stomach.

Derived from a Greek word meaning 'to lead out,' this scholarly practice of critically interpreting a text — often the Bible — also examines its historical background and literary genre — what is it called?
Exegesis: Critical investigation of a text.

Modern phylogenetics calls this a paraphyletic group covering nearly every vertebrate except the tetrapods — gill-bearing, limbless-of-digits, and usually cold-blooded. What aquatic animals are these?
Only chefs with three-plus years of rigorous training may legally prepare this potentially lethal Japanese pufferfish dish, whose poison is tetrodotoxin — what is it?
The largest of its family, this mostly solitary mammal uses long foreclaws to dig into nests and a sticky tongue to slurp up ants and termites — what animal is it?
Giant anteater: Species of mammal. The giant anteater (Myrmecophaga tridactyla) is an insectivorous mammal native to Central and South America.
Dating back roughly 250 million years to the early Triassic, this ground-dwelling insect hears through an organ on its abdomen and leaps away from danger using powerful hind legs — what is it?
Grasshopper: Common name for a group of insects.

This Austrian physician who coined "autistic psychopathy" lent his name to a syndrome, but later faced allegations he referred disabled children to a Vienna clinic that killed hundreds during the Nazi era — who was he?
Found in trace amounts in modern gasoline blends, this colorless, six-carbon alkane boils at about 69°C and serves as a cheap, low-reactivity solvent — what is it?
A colorless gas that throws off white fumes the moment it meets moist air, it turns into a familiar strong acid once dissolved in water — which compound, formula HCl?
Hydrogen chloride: Chemical compound. Hydrogen chloride gas and hydrochloric acid are important in technology and industry.
Equal to one-twelfth of a foot and derived from the Roman word for 'twelfth,' this unit of length has been pegged to exactly 25.4 millimeters since the mid-20th century — what is it?
Inch: Unit of length. The inch (symbol: in or ″) is a unit of length in the British Imperial and the United States customary systems of measurement.

The New York Times once called him "the nation's most influential evangelical leader," yet he was never an ordained minister — instead this psychologist founded Focus on the Family and led it from 1977 to 2010. Who was he?
James Dobson: American evangelical Christian psychologist and author (1936–2025)
Struggling with a morphine addiction from a Civil War saber wound, this pharmacist and chemist developed a coca-and-caffeine beverage in 1886 that became Coca-Cola — who is he?
John Stith Pemberton: American pharmacist, inventor of Coca-Cola (1831–1888)
First described in 1845 by a German physicist, these two equalities govern current and voltage in electrical networks and generalized Georg Ohm's work — what are they called?
Kirchhoff's circuit laws: Two equalities that deal with the current and potential difference.

Caused by a bacterium that thrives in fresh water and can contaminate hot tubs and water tanks, this atypical pneumonia brings cough, high fever and muscle pains days after exposure — what's it called?
Legionnaires' disease: Form of atypical pneumonia. Legionnaires' disease is a form of atypical pneumonia caused by any species of Legionella bacteria, quite often Legionella pneumophila.
Named after both a biblical sea monster and the author of 'Moby-Dick,' this extinct predatory sperm whale roamed ancient oceans roughly 9 million years ago — which genus?
Livyatan: Extinct genus of sperm whale from the Miocene epoch.
Native to northeastern Australia and first commercially grown at scale in Hawaii during the 1880s, this is the only widely cultivated food plant indigenous to Australia — what nut is it?
Macadamia: Genus of plants indigenous to Australia.
Kangaroos, koalas, and wombats all belong to this mammal group whose young are born undeveloped and finish developing in their mother's pouch — what group is it?
Marsupial: Infraclass of mammals in the clade Metatheria.
The only operational rocket-powered fighter ever fielded, this WWII German interceptor became the first piloted aircraft to exceed 1,000 km/h in level flight — which aircraft?

Messerschmitt Me 163 Komet: German rocket-powered interceptor. The Messerschmitt Me 163 Komet is a rocket-powered interceptor aircraft primarily designed and produced by the German aircraft manufacturer Messerschmitt.
Awarded the 1976 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, this University of Chicago economist championed monetarism over Keynesianism and mentored future laureates like Gary Becker — who is he?
Milton Friedman: American economist and statistician (1912–2006)
This Bangladeshi economist founded Grameen Bank and pioneered modern microcredit, winning the 2006 Nobel Peace Prize before later leading an interim government — who is he?
Muhammad Yunus: Bangladeshi economist and statesman (born 1940)
Carried harmlessly in the noses of about 10% of adults, this bacterium is the only cause of bacterial meningitis known to occur in epidemics, especially across Africa and Asia — which microbe?
Neisseria meningitidis: Species of bacterium that can cause meningitis.
Designed in the late 1950s as a privately funded project, this small twin-engine fighter was built cheap to buy and maintain, making it a hugely popular export jet — what is it?
Northrop F-5: US lightweight low-cost fighter aircraft.
Named by analogy to how organs serve the body, what term describes a specialized, function-specific subunit within a biological cell?

Organelle: Specialized subunit within a cell. The name organelle comes from the idea that these structures are parts of cells, as organs are to the body, hence organelle, the suffix -elle being a diminutive.
Often triggered by nail-biting or frequent hand-washing, this inflammation of the skin around the nail is usually bacterial when sudden and fungal when it drags on — what is it called?
Paronychia: Inflammation of skin surrounding a nail. Its sudden (acute) occurrence is usually due to the bacterium Staphylococcus aureus.

Caused by a lack of intrinsic factor — often from an autoimmune attack on the stomach — this vitamin B12 deficiency disorder brings gradual fatigue, a smooth red tongue, and numbness in the hands and feet — which condition?
Pernicious anemia: Lack of red blood cells due to vitamin B12 deficiency.
Resembling a round, tailless rabbit with short ears, this small mountain-dwelling mammal's Himalayan relative lives at elevations above 6,000 meters — what animal is it?
Pika: Genus of mountain-dwelling mammal. A pika ( PY-kə, PEE-kə) is a small, mountain-dwelling mammal native to Asia and North America.
This succulent plant in the family Portulacaceae has every part edible, whether raw or cooked, and is also known by folk names like little hogweed — what is it, scientifically speaking?
Portulaca oleracea: Species of plant in the purslane family.

This noncontagious autoimmune disease shows up as dry, scaly red or purple patches, and injuring the skin can trigger new lesions right at that spot — a quirk called the Koebner phenomenon — what is it?
Psoriasis: Autoimmune diseases of the skin. Psoriasis is a long-lasting, noncontagious autoimmune disease characterized by patches of abnormal skin.

Born Richard Alpert, this spiritual teacher researched psychedelics with Timothy Leary at Harvard before writing the 1971 bestseller Be Here Now, popularizing Eastern spirituality in the West. What name did he later take?
As chairman of Purdue Pharma, this physician-businessman oversaw the launch of OxyContin and was later portrayed in the miniseries Dopesick and Painkiller — who is he?

Formed by the fusion of five vertebrae between the ages of 18 and 30, this triangular bone sits at the base of the spine and connects to the tailbone below and the last lumbar vertebra above. What is it?
Sacrum: Bone of the spine. The sacrum situates at the upper, back part of the pelvic cavity, between the two wings of the pelvis.
Covered in a spiny shell called a test and moving via tiny tube feet, this globular ocean-floor animal grazes mostly on algae — what creature is it?
Sea urchin: Class of marine invertebrates.
This small, wingless, primitive insect gets its common name from its grey sheen and darting, fish-like movements — and its scientific name hints at a diet of sugars and starches. What is it?
